strengths: Substantial domain resource: the paper describes a multi-organ ultrasound dataset of ~208K clinical cases and ~1.47M key-frame images from 15 hospitals spanning seven anatomical systems (thyroid, breast, liver, kidney, gynecology, vessel, heart), together with multi-task annotations (report generation, diagnosis, VQA). If made accessible in some form, this would be a valuable community resource for medical multimodal NLP.

The two-stage training design is sensible and reasonably motivated: Stage I freezes the Qwen2-VL backbone and trains only the injected Dual-path MoE to avoid catastrophic forgetting, while Stage II applies LoRA plus MoE updates for cooperative instruction fine-tuning. This is a defensible engineering recipe for domain adaptation.

The empirical section has breadth: three task families evaluated across seven anatomical regions, plus ablations on the shared expert (Table 5), top-k routing (Table 6), and number of experts (Table 7), together with expert-routing distribution plots and Grad-CAM visualizations. The ablation on expert count (0/2/4 experts) is a useful diagnostic.
The paper is generally well organized and the case-study figures (Figures 7-13) give a concrete qualitative view of how generic VLMs fail on ultrasound versus the specialized model.

Honest reporting in places: for VQA the authors state the model wins 16 of 35 metric-anatomy combinations and ranks second in 10 more, and they acknowledge weak vascular performance and long-tail data issues.
weaknesses: Headline claim in the abstract is not supported by the paper's own tables. The stated "improvements of 10.15 and 4.77 points in BLEU-1 and ROUGE-1 ... compared to Qwen2-VL" match the 0-expert vs 4-expert ablation in Table 7 (43.72 -> 53.87 BLEU-1, 56.92 -> 61.69 ROUGE-1), not the Qwen2-VL comparison (Table 2 average: EchoVLM 61.69 BLEU-1 vs Qwen2-VL 9.42). The abstract therefore misattributes an ablation delta to a baseline comparison, which is a validity problem for the paper's central quantitative claim.

Internal numerical inconsistency between the main results and the ablation tables. For report generation, Table 2 reports EchoVLM averages of 61.69 BLEU-1 / 53.76 ROUGE-1, while Table 5 ("w Share Expert") and Table 7 (4 Experts) report 53.87 / 61.69 for the same task - a transposition/inconsistency that is never explained. Diagnosis numbers do line up between Tables 3 and 5, which makes the report-generation mismatch more suspicious. The reader cannot tell which numbers represent the actual model.

Confounded and under-specified baselines. EchoVLM is an 11B model compared against 7B baselines, with no parameter-matched control, so gains may reflect scale rather than the Dual-path MoE design. More critically, the strongest competitors ("LLaVA-OneVision-Ultrasound", "Qwen2-VL-Ultrasound") are never described anywhere in the method or experiments: no training data, procedure, or hyperparameters are given, even though they are the primary comparison points in Figure 1 and Tables 2-4. No comparison is made to other medical VLMs (e.g., LLaVA-Med) or to any prior ultrasound-specific model, despite the claim of being "the first universal ultrasound-specialized VLM."

Evaluation metrics are inadequate for the clinical claims being made. Report generation and diagnosis are scored only with BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore, which are known to correlate weakly with clinical correctness. There is no radiologist or expert evaluation, no analysis of clinically significant errors (missed lesions, hallucinated findings), and no safety analysis - despite framing the system as "a viable technical solution for future clinical applications."

The presented case studies contradict the claims. In Figure 9 (liver), EchoVLM outputs "no lesions found within the gallbladder cavity," while the ground truth describes a 5.5 x 2.1 cm intracytic gallbladder lesion. In Figure 13 (thyroid), EchoVLM both asserts the left lobe is normal and describes a focal lesion in it, and misses the right-lobe lesion that the ground truth reports. Yet the text describes these examples as demonstrating that the model "effectively captur[es] clinically meaningful information." Similarly, the claim of "consistently outperforms" is contradicted by per-anatomy results (e.g., vessel BLEU-1 30.29 vs 32.29 for Qwen2-VL-Ultrasound; breast METEOR 46.26 vs 46.27 and BERTScore 74.74 vs 75.24).

Reproducibility is not at Findings level. The dataset is proprietary (15 hospitals) with no release or access plan, no de-identification/IRB/ethics statement anywhere in the paper, and no discussion of data governance. The code/weights URL is truncated in the abstract ("available at" with no link). The held-out test set (27,577 images / 3,000 reports) appears to be drawn from the same sources as training, so no external validation supports the generalization claims; the observed margins could reflect institutional acquisition-style memorization.

The 1.8M instruction-tuning corpus is generated largely by LLMs (GPT-3.5-turbo, Qwen2-72B, Llama-3-70B) with expert verification of only 5% of batches. This raises unaddressed concerns about hallucinated clinical content in the training data and about the model being optimized to imitate LLM report style, which can inflate overlap metrics without improving clinical fidelity. No quality analysis of the synthetic data or its effect on clinical accuracy is provided.

Methodological novelty is limited for an NLP venue. The Dual-path MoE (frozen FFN copy + always-active shared expert + top-2 routed experts with a load-balancing auxiliary loss) is an incremental combination of DeepSeekMoE-style shared experts, standard top-k routing, and LoRA. There is no comparison against alternative MoE designs or simpler domain-adaptation baselines (e.g., full fine-tuning, LoRA-only) trained on the same data; the 0-expert condition in Table 7 is the closest thing, and its training configuration is not clearly specified.

No statistical rigor. The ablation text claims "statistically significant improvements" but no significance tests, confidence intervals, seeds, or multiple runs are reported; all inferences rest on single-run point estimates.

Related work is thin on the most relevant prior art: it does not discuss existing ultrasound-specific foundation models/VLMs, and the medical VLM discussion is limited to LLaVA-Med, which weakens the positioning of the contribution.

Minor but non-trivial reporting issues: inconsistent dataset sizes (208,941 vs 208,491 cases appear in the introduction, method, and conclusion); equation/notation inconsistency (alpha in Eq. 3 vs lambda in the training-strategy text for the same balancing role); reliance on Supplementary Material that reviewers cannot access for key pipeline details; and figure/table cross-references in the appendix that do not align with the main text.

strengths: Substantial data curation effort: a multi-center ultrasound corpus (208,941 cases, 1.47M key frames, 7 anatomical regions, 15 hospitals) is a genuinely useful resource, and the two-stage filtering protocol (image filtering + report filtering) is described concretely enough to be understood.

Broad empirical coverage: three distinct tasks (report generation, ultrasound diagnosis, VQA) are evaluated across seven anatomical regions with per-organ breakdowns, and the model is compared against four baselines, which goes beyond a single-task demonstration.

The ablation suite is well-motivated and informative: shared-expert ablation (Table 5), Top-1 vs Top-2 routing (Table 6), and expert-count scaling (Table 7) systematically probe the design choices and show consistent directional gains for the shared expert and Top-2 routing.

The paper reports concrete training configurations (Table 8: encoder, LoRA rank/alpha/dropout, learning rates, DeepSpeed ZeRO2, BF16, batch sizes, parameter counts), which materially improves reproducibility of the training recipe.

Qualitative material is unusually rich for this kind of paper: Grad-CAM visualizations, expert routing distribution plots per organ, and seven case studies with side-by-side model outputs against ground-truth reports give readers a concrete view of failure modes (e.g., over-confident measurements, hallucinated findings).

The paper is largely honest about limitations: it explicitly notes underperformance on vascular analysis due to long-tailed data distribution, acknowledges VQA as an open problem, and reports that attention still drifts to non-informative regions (edges, black areas).

The Dual-path MoE formulation is described with explicit equations (Eqs. 1-9), including the load-balancing auxiliary loss and the α-modulated combination of generic and domain-specific pathways, making the architecture easy to reimplement.
weaknesses: Internal numerical inconsistency in the headline claim: the abstract states 'improvements of 10.15 and 4.77 points in BLEU-1 and ROUGE-1 compared to Qwen2-VL on the ultrasound report generation task,' but Table 7 shows 10.15 BLEU-1 and 4.77 ROUGE-1 as the 0-expert→4-expert ablation gain, not the gap over Qwen2-VL. Table 2's average row (EchoVLM 61.69 vs. Qwen2-VL 9.42) implies a far larger difference. The headline numbers appear misattributed, and the per-organ values do not obviously reconcile with the reported averages. This is a correctness problem, not a cosmetic one.

Table 2 (and Tables 3-4) are ambiguous and hard to verify: column headers mix base models, an unexplained '-Ultrasound' variant, and a '(TB)' suffix; the same baseline appears with different scores across tables (e.g., Fig. 1 vs. Table 2), and it is never stated how the '-Ultrasound' baselines were produced (same data? same schedule? same number of epochs?). Without this, the central comparison is not interpretable.

Methodological novelty is limited. A frozen copy of the pretrained FFN as a static expert, a shared always-active expert, and top-k routed experts is essentially the standard DeepSeekMoE/LLaVA-MoE-style design; the 'Dual-path' framing is a relabeling rather than a new mechanism. No MoE-based VLM baselines (e.g., MoE-LLaVA, LLaVA-MoE) or other medical/ultrasound VLMs (LLaVA-Med, ultrasound-specific foundation models) are compared against, so the claim that the MoE is responsible for the gains is not isolated.

Evaluation is inappropriate for the clinical claims made. BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore are weak proxies for clinical correctness, and no radiologist/human evaluation, no clinical-accuracy or factuality metric, and no statistical testing or multi-seed variance are reported. Yet the abstract claims 'substantial potential to enhance diagnostic accuracy,' which the evidence cannot support. The 5%-batch expert sampling in the data pipeline is also a weak guarantee for 'maintaining clinical accuracy through expert oversight.'

Reproducibility of the primary contribution is constrained: the dataset (the paper's first listed contribution) is hospital-sourced and presumably not releasable, and the code/weights link is truncated in the abstract. Baselines' training protocols, prompting templates, and the held-out test set construction (27,577 images / 3,000 reports) are only partly described, with key details deferred to a supplement.

Efficiency claims are unsupported. The abstract motivates the work by 'low efficiency across multi-task diagnostics,' but no latency, throughput, FLOPs, or memory comparison against baselines is reported, even though the model is 11B total parameters with 3.4B trainable. The 'improving both efficiency and precision' claim therefore has no evidence behind it.

The routing analysis may undercut the specialization claim. Figure 5 shows near-uniform expert utilization across layers and organs, and the text notes image tokens dominate dispatch because images outnumber reports ~7:1. Near-uniform routing is not evidence that experts specialize in 'distinct diagnostic domains'; the paper does not test whether expert assignment correlates with anatomy or task, which would be the natural analysis.

VQA results are mixed (EchoVLM beats baselines in only about half of the metric-anatomy cells, and loses on BLEU-1 average to Qwen2-VL-Ultrasound), but the paper frames this as overall success without a careful discussion of where and why it fails; likewise the strong underperformance on vessel (BLEU-1 29.54 vs. 43.58 for LLaVA-OneVision-Ultrasound) deserves more than a one-sentence long-tail explanation.

Related work is thin on ultrasound-specific and concurrent medical VLM literature, and the paper does not situate the MoE design against the MoE-VLM line of work it most closely resembles. There is also no dedicated limitations/ethics section addressing clinical deployment risk, despite the case studies showing hallucinated measurements.

strengths: Curates a large-scale, multi-organ ultrasound dataset (208,941 cases / 1.47M images across seven anatomical regions) and documents a multi-stage filtering and de-duplication protocol; if verifiable, this is a resource of genuine potential value.

Proposes a systematic instruction-tuning data generation pipeline (open/closed template split, GPT/Qwen/Llama generation, ROUGE-L/SimHash dedup, LLM screening plus expert validation) that is described in more operational detail than is typical in this space.
Ablation studies (Tables 5–7 on shared expert, Top-k routing, and number of experts) are sensibly organized and give some insight into the MoE design choices.
Strong gains on the Ultrasound Diagnosis task (Table 3) relative to the reported baselines, and competitive report-generation results.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is seriously compromised for a paper whose headline contribution is the dataset. No dataset release, no IRB/ethics statement, no de-identification or consent details for a 15-hospital clinical corpus, and the abstract's code/model link is truncated ("available at"). None of the claimed artifacts can be verified or reused.

Numerical inconsistencies between the abstract and the tables. The abstract claims "improvements of 10.15 and 4.77 points in BLEU-1 and ROUGE-1 ... compared to Qwen2-VL," but Table 2 gives average BLEU-1 61.69 vs 49.77 (≈ +11.9) and ROUGE-1 63.96 vs 58.82 (≈ +5.1). The "+10.15 BLEU-1" figure is then reused in the expert-number ablation, which suggests the reported deltas are not reliably traced to their source.

Critical baselines are missing. LLaVA-Med is explicitly named as "a representative framework" for medical VLMs but appears in none of Tables 2–4. The reported "Ultrasound" baselines (LLaVA-OneVision-Ultrasound, Qwen2-VL-Ultrasound) are central to the comparison yet there is no description of how they were trained, tuned, or matched in data/compute, so the head-to-head numbers are not interpretable.

Evaluation relies exclusively on BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore, which are known to be weak proxies for clinical fidelity. The paper nonetheless claims to provide "a viable technical solution for future clinical applications" without any radiologist/clinical assessment of factual correctness, hallucination rate, or diagnostic agreement.

VQA results (Table 4) are effectively tied or worse than baselines on METEOR, ROUGE-L, and BERTScore, yet the text frames the task as a success ("surpassing the baselines in 16 of 35 ... ranking second in an additional 10"), which is selective reporting rather than a supported claim.

The case studies appear cherry-picked and in at least one case contradict the narrative. In Figure 7 the ground truth describes a 24×21 mm anechoic area and a 44×33 mm ovarian mass, and the two "-Ultrasound" baselines mention the anechoic area, whereas EchoVLM reports "ovaries were clear bilaterally, and no abnormal masses were found" — i.e., a missed finding presented as an advantage.

Limited methodological novelty. The "Dual-path MoE" (frozen FFN anchor + shared always-active expert + Top-2 routed LoRA experts with an auxiliary load-balancing loss) is a recombination of existing MoE/shared-expert designs; the contribution is largely domain application rather than a new mechanism.

Overclaiming throughout: "first ten-billion-parameter universal ultrasound-specialized VLM," "largest multi-organ ultrasound dataset to date," "seamless integration ... into clinical workflows," none of which are supported by the evidence presented.

Presentation and rigor problems: "We pioneering propose"; Figure 2 caption omits gynecology although the figure shows it; a dangling reference "Zhang et al. (?)" in the visualization section; and the synthetic data pipeline (GPT-3.5/Qwen2-72B/Llama-3.1-70B) raises potential contamination and quality-control questions that are not addressed.
Relevance to ACL/NLP is marginal: the core contribution is a medical imaging application, and the NLP-relevant methodological content (MoE routing, LoRA) is standard.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely under-served domain (ultrasound) with a large, multi-organ, multi-center corpus (208,941 cases, 1.47M images, 7 anatomical systems, 15 hospitals) and a documented expert-validated instruction-tuning pipeline, which is a substantial data-curation contribution for the medical VLM community.

Evaluation is broad and reasonably rigorous: 12 generic/medical VLM baselines, three task families (report generation, diagnosis, VQA), five NLP metrics plus entity-level recognition metrics, ablations on the shared expert, Top-k routing, and number of experts, and an out-of-distribution test on a public dataset to probe generalization.

The Dual-path MoE design (frozen copied FFN as a static anchor + shared expert + top-2 routed experts, with a load-balancing loss and two-stage frozen-then-LoRA training) is clearly specified with equations, hyperparameters (Table 9), and routing-distribution analysis (Figure 8), making the method largely reproducible from the description.

Ablations are informative and candid: Top-2 vs Top-1 routing, 0/2/4/6 experts with training-time trade-offs, and the shared-expert contribution are all quantified, and the paper reports per-anatomy behavior rather than only aggregate numbers.

Qualitative evidence (Grad-CAM visualizations, per-system case studies with ground-truth reports) supports the quantitative claims and helps the reader judge clinical plausibility; code and model weights are stated to be released.
Limitations section is honest about vascular underperformance, long-tail data distribution, and VQA weakness versus Lingshu, which strengthens credibility.
weaknesses: Reproducibility of the core data contribution is limited: the 15-hospital dataset is not released and only code/weights are promised. Since the dataset is central to the claims, the community cannot verify the curation, the instruction-tuning data, or the reported held-out evaluation, which is a serious constraint for a Findings-level reproducibility standard.

Comparison fairness is questionable. The paper states baselines follow 'full-parameter fine-tuning,' while EchoVLM uses frozen backbone + LoRA + MoE. This conflates architecture gains with training-regime gains, and the report-generation margins (e.g., 7.58 BLEU-1) may partly reflect the different tuning paradigm rather than domain specialization.

Overclaimed novelty and internal inconsistency. 'First universal ultrasound-specialized VLM' is asserted despite the paper itself citing EchoCLIP, KMVE, FetalCLIP, Sonomate, and EchoPrime, several of which are ultrasound-specialized VLMs. The parameter count is described inconsistently as '10-billion,' 'tens of billions,' and 3B/11B variants across the abstract and introduction.

Statistical significance is never established: single-run numbers are reported with no seeds, variance, or significance tests, yet many comparisons differ by well under one point, making some 'SOTA' claims fragile.

Language/NLP contribution is modest and the CL relevance is thin: the paper is essentially a medical-imaging systems paper with report generation and VQA as downstream tasks; there is little analysis of the linguistic/structured-report aspects that would distinguish it from a general domain-adaptation result.

The expert-validation and desensitization claims are asserted but under-documented (e.g., 40,000-sample clinical validation is mentioned without inter-annotator agreement, error rates, or how validation disagreements were adjudicated), which weakens the dataset-quality argument.

Writing and presentation are dense and at times unclear; some tables (e.g., Table 1 dataset summary, Table 8/10 entity metrics) are hard to parse, and multiple claims (e.g., 'tens of billions of parameters') are left uncorrected.

strengths: Substantial data resource: the paper curates a large multi-organ ultrasound corpus (208,941 clinical cases, 1.47M key-frame images, 7 anatomical systems, 15 hospitals, 100+ diseases/findings) and documents a careful, expert-validated few-shot prompting pipeline that yields 1.8M instruction-tuning pairs. This is a meaningful contribution to the medical VLM community.

Comprehensive and multi-faceted evaluation: the authors report results across report generation, ultrasound diagnosis, and VQA against 12 generic and medical-specific VLMs, and supplement this with OOD evaluation on a public dataset, fine-grained entity-level recognition metrics (Tables 8, 10, 12), routing-distribution analysis (Fig. 8), and Grad-CAM visualization (Fig. 9). The inclusion of entity-level metrics and OOD tests is a genuine methodological strength for clinical NLP.

Sensible architecture/training design: the Dual-path MoE (frozen FFN anchor + shared expert + routed experts) with a two-stage parameter-isolated pre-training followed by cooperative LoRA fine-tuning is a reasonable way to inject domain knowledge without catastrophic forgetting, and the ablations on shared expert, Top-k routing, and expert count (Tables 5–7) provide some support for the design choices.

The problem is well-motivated and clinically relevant, and the paper is generally clearly written and organized, with an informative related-work comparison (Table 1) that contextualizes the contribution against existing ultrasound datasets.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the system largely integrates existing ingredients (LLaVA-style training, LoRA, Mixture-of-Experts, self-instruct/few-shot prompting). The repeated 'first open-source 10B ultrasound VLM' framing is difficult to substantiate given prior ultrasound-specialized VLMs (EchoCLIP, FetalCLIP, Sonomate) and is more marketing than technical novelty.

Reproducibility of the central contribution is uncertain: the core asset is proprietary clinical data from 15 hospitals. The abstract promises 'source code and model weights,' but no location/link is given, and it is unclear whether the dataset (the paper's main claimed contribution) can be released. If neither data nor a detailed data-construction recipe is available, the headline contribution is not independently reproducible, even if model weights allow partial evaluation.

Clinical validity is not rigorously established. Expert verification is applied to the training data and to a sampled subset of generated data, but there is no blinded radiologist evaluation of the final model's outputs (e.g., factual correctness, safety, or hallucination rate on the held-out test set). For a clinical decision-support claim, this is a significant gap, and BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore—which the authors themselves acknowledge correlate imperfectly with clinical correctness—still carry much of the headline evidence.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting: 'SOTA' claims rest on single runs, and margins over strong baselines are sometimes small (e.g., Table 4 VQA where several baselines are competitive, and the model trails Lingshu on VQA in some categories). Without confidence intervals or multiple seeds, the strength of the comparative claims is hard to gauge.

Internal consistency issues that should be checked: the introduction says 'tens of billions of parameters' while the models are 3B/11B; and some numbers cited in the running text (e.g., BERTScore values for breast/kidney) do not obviously match the corresponding table entries, suggesting either OCR/table-formatting problems or text-table mismatches that need correction.

The core two-stage training strategy is not directly ablated (e.g., against full fine-tuning or a single-stage MoE training), so the specific benefit of the proposed pipeline over simpler alternatives is not isolated. Additionally, the MoE ablations are mixed—the shared expert and Top-2 routing actually reduce VQA BLEU-1 (Tables 5–6)—so the claimed uniform benefit of the architecture is overstated.

Fairness/strength of baselines is unclear: all baselines are fully fine-tuned on the same corpus under the LLaVA paradigm, which may not reflect their optimal adaptation and could disadvantage very large models; conversely, EchoVLM benefits from the largest proprietary corpus and MoE capacity, so the comparisons conflate data scale, architecture, and training recipe.

strengths: Curates a large multi-organ ultrasound dataset (208,941 cases, 1.47M key-frame images, 1.8M instruction-tuning pairs) and a multi-task instruction-generation pipeline, which could be a valuable resource if properly released and validated.

Proposes a Dual-path MoE architecture with shared and routed experts to inject ultrasound-specific knowledge while preserving generic vision-language knowledge, supported by a two-stage training strategy and ablations on shared experts, Top-k routing, and expert number.
Evaluates across seven anatomical systems, multiple tasks (report generation, diagnosis, VQA), and several general/medical VLMs, including entity-level and out-of-distribution evaluations.
Addresses clinically relevant ultrasound tasks and includes qualitative case studies and Grad-CAM visualizations, suggesting practical potential.
weaknesses: Evaluation validity is weak for core tasks: VQA and ultrasound diagnosis are evaluated mainly with BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore rather than accuracy/exact match or clinician judgment. The VQA table in particular lacks task-appropriate correctness metrics, so the claim of superior VQA performance is not adequately supported.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code/model/data link is provided despite claiming availability, the main clinical dataset is not released, data generation depends on proprietary LLM/VLM pools and expert validation, and patient/hospital-level train-test splitting and leakage controls are not described.

Baseline comparisons are not convincingly fair: the paper states all baselines follow LLaVA-style full-parameter fine-tuning, but does not document training data, prompts, compute, or optimization details for baselines; comparisons between 7B baselines and 11B EchoVLM are not controlled, and some baselines may not have received the same in-domain instruction data.

Strong claims such as 'first open-source 10-billion-parameter ultrasound-tailored VLM' and 'largest multi-organ ultrasound dataset' are not adequately supported. Prior ultrasound VLMs and datasets are discussed (e.g., EchoPrime, EchoCLIP, FetalCLIP, Sonmate, KMVE), and Table 1 itself shows larger video/image counts for some existing resources, making the 'largest' claim questionable.

The Dual-path MoE contribution is incremental and insufficiently differentiated from existing MoE designs (e.g., shared-expert MoE variants). There is no direct ablation against a standard MoE, LoRA-only fine-tuning, or full fine-tuning to isolate the claimed benefit.

Technical reporting is inconsistent: the abstract says 10B parameters, results use EchoVLM (11B), and the text refers to 'tens of billions'; parameter counts and training configurations are unclear or contradictory.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multi-run variance is reported. Results are single-run and lack human evaluation of generated reports or diagnostic outputs, despite clinical claims.

The data-generation pipeline relies heavily on synthetic instructions from GPT-3.5/4, Qwen2, Llama-3, etc.; quality control is only partially validated (40k samples) and no full audit of hallucinations or clinical safety is provided.
Out-of-distribution evaluation is limited and does not establish robust clinical generalization; the paper acknowledges poor vascular performance but does not resolve it.
Presentation issues remain: future-dated references, typographical inconsistencies, and important methodological details placed only in the appendix make the main claims harder to verify.
